BXL-2425-00031-v9.headline: Cut Brussels MPs' parliamentary indemnity by 5% on a permanent basis, applying the reduction not only to the base pay but also to the extra indemnities paid for special functions.
BXL-2425-00031-v9.proposed_by: Francis Dagrin, Oliver Rittweger de Moor, Francoise De Smedt, Jan Busselen (PTB/PVDA)
BXL-2425-00031-v9.source_brief:
On the table is a standalone proposal to reduce the indemnity Brussels regional MPs draw by 5% as a lasting measure, and to push that cut further than the parallel cross-party text by also shaving 5% off the top-up indemnities paid to members who hold special functions (such as Bureau seats).

- **What it changes:** a 5% reduction on the base parliamentary indemnity, framed as permanent rather than time-limited, plus the same 5% applied to special-function indemnities.
- **The money cited:** speakers describe a Brussels MP's net monthly pay as more than 7,000 euros, and special-function holders receiving roughly 2,500 euros extra.
- **The wider frame:** it lands amid a regional budget described as a 1.6 to 1.9 billion euro deficit, with cuts cited to associations (15%) and family allowances.
- **The rub:** whether elected members should cut their own pay deeply and permanently as a credibility signal, or whether a 5% trim risks underpaying the job and should align with other parliaments rather than go furthest.
deep_facts: The text is proposal for a decision A-103/1 - 2024/2025, tabled to reduce the indemnities of Brussels MPs by 5%; it was deposited before the parallel Bureau text and is described by its backers as going further (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

A competing text, A-150/1 - 2024/2025, was brought by the president on behalf of the Bureau, introducing a 'retenue temporaire de 5%' (temporary 5% retention) on the parliamentary indemnity from the first payment of the 2025-2026 session; the two were debated jointly but voted separately (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Backers of A-103 argued for two differences from the Bureau text: removing the 'temporary' character (making the cut lasting), and extending the 5% reduction to indemnities for special functions, not just the base indemnity (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
A Brussels MP's pay is described in debate as 'plus de 7.000 euros nets par mois', characterised by one speaker as making them 'les parlementaires les mieux payes de Belgique' (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Special-function indemnities are described as an extra figure of about '2.500 euros supplementaires' per holder; A-103's backers favour abolishing them and at minimum applying the 5% cut to them (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Backers note the Chamber of Representatives and the Flemish Parliament temporarily reduced their members' indemnity to 95% of the base salary of a 'conseiller d'Etat sans anciennete'; the Bureau text aligns Brussels on a 100% base, applying its 5% in that logic (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
Backers state that by renouncing their end-of-term departure indemnities in June 2024, their group allowed the Brussels Parliament to save 730.000 euros (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The debate situates the measure within a regional deficit cited at '1,6 a 1,9 milliard d'euros' for 2025 and a consolidated debt that 'avoisinerait les 16,5 milliards d'euros'; cited parallel cuts include a 15% reduction in association budgets and the removal of a 10-euro top-up in family allowances for children born before 1 December 2019 (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

A Bureau majority (cited as MR, Groen, Les Engages, Open Vld, N-VA) had a month earlier tabled a note to modernise the Parliament and cut its spending by 10%, bringing its budget to a figure cited at 62 million euros (from 57-59 million in 2024, having reached 14 twelfths / about 69 million in 2025 with provisional twelfths) (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Already-applied Bureau measures cited include scrapping the chauffeured car for the presidency, removing advantages for honorary MPs, ending staff provision for the outgoing president, and ending phone-cost reimbursement for Bureau members and group chairs (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
The PTB's longstanding stated position is to halve MPs' salaries; the 5% cut and the special-functions extension are presented as steps short of that demand (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Several groups (Ecolo, Team Fouad Ahidar, DeFI) voiced support for the substance of A-103 as more coherent or 'linear' than the Bureau text, since many members sit on neither the Bureau nor the enlarged Bureau; others (Groen) signalled they could abstain to respect the broader cross-party accord (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Tied debates flagged for future work: a 2014 rule change letting a single member form (and chair) a group with the attached costs; remunerating special functions on the basis of effective attendance; and a DeFI proposal to cut the number of MPs from 89 to 60 (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
BXL-2425-00031-v9.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference - not stated verbatim in the record)*

- Two texts on the same 5% let members separate the gesture from its depth: backing the consensus Bureau cut while voting down the 'further' text lets a member claim the headline reduction without touching special-function pay or making it permanent.
- 'Temporary vs permanent' is the real wedge: a time-limited retention can quietly lapse, so insisting on permanence converts a symbolic signal into a structural pay change - which is precisely why it draws more resistance.
- Extending the cut to special-function indemnities reallocates pain toward members who hold Bureau and leadership seats, i.e. often the very people negotiating the Bureau consensus - a redistribution within the chamber, not just a cut.
- Framing pay against a billion-euro deficit and cuts to associations and family allowances builds an equity argument (the chamber should bleed before citizens do); opponents counter that an attractive indemnity keeps the mandate open to non-wealthy candidates and avoids a 'race to the bottom'.
- Voting against this text is not the same as opposing any cut, since a parallel consensus reduction exists - it can read instead as preferring alignment with other parliaments over going furthest.
BXL-2425-00031-v9.raw_fr: Proposition de decision A-103/1 - 2024/2025 visant a reduire les indemnites des parlementaires bruxellois de 5 %. Au-dela d'une baisse de 5 % de l'indemnite de base, le texte propose d'aller un cran plus loin en l'appliquant aussi aux indemnites pour fonctions speciales et en supprimant le caractere temporaire de la mesure. Les deux propositions (A-103 et celle du Bureau) ont fait l'objet d'une discussion conjointe mais d'un vote separe.

BXL-2425-00031-v1.headline: Order a Brussels battle plan against the invasive Asian hornet: one agency in charge, nests removed, bees and beekeepers protected.
BXL-2425-00031-v1.proposed_by: Jonathan de Patoul (DéFI) and co-signers across multiple groups
BXL-2425-00031-v1.source_brief:
The Asian hornet (Vespa velutina nigrithorax) arrived in Brussels in 2018 and has spread exponentially: fire-brigade callouts for nests jumped from 20 in 2020 to 670 in 2023, and each nest devours an average twelve kilos of insects per year — 60% of them bees. This resolution asks the government to put a proper plan in place.

- **What it asks for:** listing the hornet on the Brussels invasive-species register, designating a single coordinating body (proposed candidate: Bruxelles Environnement) for nest neutralisation, launching awareness campaigns, and clarifying when fire-brigade removal is free of charge.
- **Why bees matter:** speakers stress that honeybees and solitary bees pollinate the majority of our food crops; their collapse would cascade through the food chain. Urban solitary bees in Brussels are already under pressure from hard surfaces and density.
- **Who pays today:** removing a nest costs 250–1,000 euros; the total regional cost was estimated between 170,000 and 700,000 euros; current fire-brigade rules are unclear about the threshold for free intervention, which risks under-reporting.
- **The rub:** whether a non-binding resolution will actually unlock resources and a named coordinating agency, or whether it becomes another unfunded commitment while nests keep multiplying.
deep_facts: The Asian hornet (Vespa velutina nigrithorax) was first detected in Brussels Region in 2018; it has been on the EU list of invasive exotic species of concern since 13 July 2016, and is cited as having been accidentally introduced in France in 2004 (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Fire-brigade interventions for Asian-hornet nests in Brussels rose from 20 in 2020 to approximately 670 in 2023; one speaker noted 89 nests were counted in a single 4-square-kilometre stretch of Woluwe-Saint-Pierre alone (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Each nest consumes an average of twelve kilos of insects per year, of which 60% are bees; a single founding queen can produce 200 to 500 new founding queens annually, creating an exponential reproduction curve (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

About 30% of nests are located less than ten metres from the ground, creating direct public-safety risks; a nest fell from a cornice in Etterbeek onto a public street near a grocery shop; in France fatalities from swarm attacks have been recorded (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The cost of destroying a single nest ranges from 250 to 1,000 euros; the total regional bill was estimated between 170,000 and 700,000 euros per year; some residents still bear removal costs themselves, which discourages reporting (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

An existing convention limits free Siamu (Brussels fire service) intervention to cases meeting a 'serious immediate danger' criterion, but the threshold is unclear — e.g., whether a nest at 30 metres qualifies as 'less than seven metres from a school' criterion (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The resolution calls for the hornet to be added to the Brussels invasive-species list, an action plan to be drawn up, a single reference body for nest management to be designated, and awareness campaigns to be launched including guidance for municipal officials (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The PTB, while voting for the resolution, argued the Siamu already lacks the staffing and equipment for this additional environmental mission and called for a dedicated public-sector unit — such as a specialised Bruxelles Environnement brigade — rather than shifting costs to private contractors (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
Team Fouad Ahidar called for nest removal to be free for low-income households and proposed spring queen-trapping citizen initiatives as a low-cost complementary tool (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The MR withdrew its co-signature from the text, citing a party decision not to co-sign with certain other groups, but confirmed its substantive support and voted for the resolution (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
BXL-2425-00031-v1.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The 20-to-670 intervention curve in three years is the political engine: it turns an environmental niche issue into a public-order and budget issue, broadening the coalition to parties otherwise indifferent to biodiversity.
- Naming 'a single coordinating body' is the load-bearing ask — diffuse responsibility across communes, fire service and Bruxelles Environnement is precisely why the problem has grown unchecked; the resolution's value depends entirely on whether government follows through with a named entity and a budget line.
- The free-removal question carries a social-equity dimension: residents who cannot afford 250–1,000 euros per nest will under-report, concentrating infestations in lower-income neighbourhoods with older housing stock and fewer green-space managers.
- A non-binding resolution has low enforcement teeth; the real test is whether the incoming government treats it as an instruction or a decoration.
BXL-2425-00031-v1.raw_fr: La proposition de resolution demande au gouvernement bruxellois d'etablir un plan de prevention et de lutte contre la proliferation du frelon asiatique (Vespa velutina nigrithorax), apparu pour la premiere fois en Region bruxelloise en 2018. Les interventions des pompiers pour des nids sont passees de 20 en 2020 a pres de 670 en 2023. Le texte reclame l'inscription de l'espece sur la liste bruxelloise des especes invasives, la designation d'un acteur de reference unique pour la neutralisation des nids, des campagnes de sensibilisation et la clarification des conditions d'intervention gratuite.

BXL-2425-00031-v5.headline: Make 11 July an official Brussels day of remembrance of the Srebrenica genocide, with annual commemorations and education in schools.
BXL-2425-00031-v5.proposed_by: Leila Agic (PS), Ahmed Laaouej (PS), Zakia Khattabi (Ecolo), Stijn Bex (Groen), Fouad Ahidar (Team Fouad Ahidar) and co-signers
BXL-2425-00031-v5.source_brief:
Thirty years after more than 8,372 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were executed at Srebrenica in July 1995 — the worst mass atrocity on European soil since World War II — the UN General Assembly in 2024 proclaimed 11 July as an International Day of Reflection and Commemoration. This resolution asks Brussels Region to apply that commitment locally.

- **What it asks for:** official recognition of 11 July as a regional commemoration day; encouragement for communes and the government to organise annual ceremonies, expositions and educational actions; solidarity with the Mothers of Srebrenica and survivor associations; and support for a new commemorative plaque in the Rue de Bosnie in Saint-Gilles, unveiled the day after the plenary vote.
- **The controversy:** some speakers used the debate to draw a parallel with the ongoing conflict in Gaza; one group, objecting to that linkage, filed an amendment (later withdrawn) to strengthen the territorial link, and in plenary cited objections to the Gaza references — though it ultimately withdrew its amendment, and a second amendment was greeted with applause across the chamber.
- **Amendment 2:** adding support for the Saint-Gilles commemorative plaque initiative; Amendment 1 (proposing the Rue de Bosnie as a formal memorial space) was withdrawn before the vote.
- **The rub:** whether a regional parliament should go beyond territorial competences to make sweeping solidarity statements on active conflicts, or whether the duty of memory obligates exactly that.
deep_facts: The UN General Assembly proclaimed 11 July as the International Day of Reflection and Commemoration of the Genocide Committed in Srebrenica in 1995 in a resolution adopted in 2024; the Brussels text applies that recognition at the regional level (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The massacre took place between 11 and 16 July 1995; 8,372 men and boys are named on the memorial at Potocari; the youngest victim, Fatima Muhic, was born and died on the same day at the Potocari school, a UN-designated safe zone (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The Srebrenica massacre has been recognised as genocide by the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY); Belgium recognised it early, aligning with the EU and UN position (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The broader Balkan wars produced more than 100,000 dead in Bosnia, 20,000 in Croatia, over 13,000 in Kosovo, an estimated 20,000 women subjected to sexual violence, and hundreds of thousands of displaced persons and refugees (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
An estimated 7,600 persons remain listed as missing in Bosnia-Herzegovina; psychological trauma, described as trans-generational, continues across Balkan societies (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The MR filed Amendment 1 to point 1 of the dispositif, proposing to identify the Rue de Bosnie in Saint-Gilles as a memorial site and provide for a commemorative artwork; this amendment was withdrawn before the vote, with the chair thanking Mme Bytyçi (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Amendment 2 — tabled by the PS, supporting the Saint-Gilles commune initiative to unveil a commemorative plaque in the Rue de Bosnie on 11 July 2025 — was greeted with general applause when put to the vote (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

In the final explanations of vote, one member (Mme Clémentine Barzin, MR) voiced two reservations: the tenuous link with regional competences, and an objection to the method of drafting, specifically the inclusion of a Gaza parallel in a text about a recognised past genocide (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Several speakers (PS, Ecolo, Team Fouad Ahidar, Groen) explicitly connected the Srebrenica duty of memory to the current situation in Gaza; Ecolo stated 'tout acte de violence de masse et toute atteinte disproportionnee a des populations civiles doivent etre denonces' (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The day after the plenary, 11 July 2025, marked the first official international commemoration day; the PTB argued genuine peace comes not through military alliances but through social justice and solidarity (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
BXL-2425-00031-v5.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The Gaza sub-debate is the political fault line: linking a recognised historical genocide to an active, contested conflict is factually and legally fraught, and the MR's single abstention — rather than a no vote — is a calibrated signal that it supports the memory obligation but objects to the editorial choices.
- Withdrawing Amendment 1 (MR's memorial-site proposal) reads as a de-escalation to avoid a fracture on what should be a unifying text; it let the assembly end on general applause for Amendment 2 — a classic parliamentary face-saving move.
- The timing — eve of the 30th anniversary, day before the Saint-Gilles plaque unveiling — transforms the abstract resolution into a concrete civic moment, giving the vote the resonance a purely symbolic text would lack.
- Drafting a regional commemoration text that stays within territorial competences while satisfying groups that view the resolution's value as precisely its universalist reach is structurally impossible — the abstention proves the tension is real.
BXL-2425-00031-v5.raw_fr: La proposition de resolution invite la Region bruxelloise a appliquer la resolution de l'Assemblee generale des Nations unies proclamant le 11 juillet comme journee internationale de reflexion et de commemoration du genocide commis a Srebrenica en 1995. Elle demande que le 11 juillet soit integre dans les actions de sensibilisation regionales, que les initiatives de memoire soient soutenues et que soit exprimee la solidarite avec les familles des victimes et les survivants. Un amendement no 2, soutenant l'initiative de la commune de Saint-Gilles d'inaugurer une plaque commemorative rue de Bosnie le lendemain, a egalement ete mis aux voix.

BXL-2425-00031-v7.headline: Merge Brussels's scattered job-support schemes for people with disabilities into one system — wage subsidies, grants and traineeships under Actiris, equal for French and Dutch speakers.
BXL-2425-00031-v7.proposed_by: Joëlle Maison (DéFI), Emile Luhahi (Groen), Imane Belguenani (Open Vld), Farida Tahar (Ecolo), Fadila Laanan (PS), Pascal Smet (Vooruit.brussels), Stéphanie Lange (Les Engagés), Sadik Köksal (MR)
BXL-2425-00031-v7.source_brief:
Only 33% of Brusselers with a disability are employed, against a 50% European average. This text transfers competences from the Phare service (under the French Community Commission) to Actiris, the regional employment body, unifying two previously separate aid streams — the Phare insertion premium and the Activa 'reduced capacity' premium — into a single coherent scheme applicable to French and Dutch speakers alike.

- **What changes:** a single wage-subsidy calculated on estimated productivity loss (10–75% of a reference salary), a new self-employment creation grant, discovery and training internships, and auxiliary aids for workplace adaptations; public employers that have not met their disability-quota obligations are excluded from the new benefits.
- **The NL equity fix:** since 2019, Dutch-speaking Bruxellois with a disability have had no access to these aids — the ordinance closes that gap.
- **The critics' objection:** the core logic of measuring a person's eligibility against their 'productivity loss' forces those already excluded by society to prove their worth against the very standard that marginalises them; the text also lacks binding quotas with sanctions, no formal appeals mechanism, and was voted less than two weeks after tabling without formal consultation of the Brussels Council for Persons with Disabilities.
- **The rub:** whether incentive-based wage subsidies conditional on productivity assessments are the right lever for inclusion, or whether only enforceable quotas with sanctions — as in the French public-sector model where 6% of staff have a disability — will close the gap.
deep_facts: Article 22ter of the Belgian Constitution, inserted on 12 March 2021, guarantees every person with a disability the right to full inclusion in society, including the right to reasonable accommodations; the ordinance is presented as a regional implementation of that constitutional right (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The employment rate of Bruxellois with a disability is cited at 33% (one speaker cites 27.7% for the Brussels-specific figure against a 57.3% overall rate in the Region, a gap of nearly 30 percentage points), against a 50% European average; the poverty-risk rate for a Belgian with a disability is 22%, compared to 12% for the general population (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Since 2019, Dutch-speaking Bruxellois with a disability have had no access to employment aids; the ordinance restores equal access by bringing all Brussels residents under a single Actiris-administered scheme (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Five aid mechanisms are created: (1) a wage intervention calculated on estimated productivity loss (10–75% of a reference salary); (2) a self-employment creation and maintenance premium; (3) discovery internships (unpaid); (4) training internships and auxiliary aids covering workplace adaptations, equipment and travel costs; (5) a transitional support for those combining both former schemes (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The expression 'perte de rendement' (productivity loss) was acknowledged by the main proposer to be uncomfortable but legally required: EU state-aid rules demand that a subsidy compensates for a measurable economic loss; 'loss of autonomy' alone does not suffice as justification under those rules (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The Brussels Council for Persons with Disabilities (CBPH) issued an emergency advisory opinion the day before the plenary vote stating it had not been formally consulted; proposers replied that multiple contacts occurred in 2023 and 2025 and committed to formal consultation on implementing decrees (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Public-sector employers that have not met their statutory disability-quota obligations (adopted unanimously in parliament about a decade ago but widely unmet due to lack of sanctions) are excluded from eligibility for the new subsidies (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
The NGO Diversicom estimated the public-finance gain of moving a person with a disability into employment at slightly more than 30,000 euros (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

PTB criticised the text for being tabled under urgency: the Conseil d'Etat gave no opinion (as it was a proposition, not a projet), the CBPH gave no formal opinion, and the interval between tabling and plenary vote was under two weeks; one PTB speaker argued this violated the disability-rights principle 'nothing about us without us' (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

N-VA expressed concern that the existing Actiris budget transferred from Phare (slightly over 1 million euros, previously underused) may be insufficient once the scheme becomes better known and more accessible — a budget risk given that no government with full powers exists to attach a financial plan (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
BXL-2425-00031-v7.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The NL-equity fix is the political accelerant: it transforms a technical subsidy reform into a rights-restoration story, generating cross-party support that a mere consolidation of Francophone instruments would never have achieved.
- The PTB abstention is ideologically coherent, not obstructionist: their critique (productivity-loss framework penalises the already marginalised) is a legitimate structural objection, not a procedural complaint — they are voting on principle, not in protest at the process.
- Piloting the scheme through Actiris rather than a new body is institutionally pragmatic but carries a competence-transfer risk: Phare has decades of specialised knowledge that Actiris staff may not replicate quickly, and the lack of an appeals mechanism means service failures will be harder to challenge.
- The 'no formal government = no implementing decrees' problem is the real procedural tension: the ordinance's operational value is zero without the government arretes, and the parliament must pass a separate resolution to nudge a caretaker government into action.
BXL-2425-00031-v7.raw_fr: La proposition d'ordonnance instaure un regime unifie d'aides a l'emploi pour les personnes en situation de handicap en Region bruxelloise, transferant les competences du service Phare vers Actiris. Elle cree cinq mecanismes d'aide — prime d'insertion, prime pour independants, stages de decouverte et de formation, aides auxiliaires — calcules sur la base du pourcentage de perte de rendement estimee. Elle remedie egalement a l'inegalite d'acces qui prive depuis 2019 les Bruxellois neerlandophones en situation de handicap de ces dispositifs.

BXL-2425-00031-v13.headline: Trim Brussels MPs' pay by 5% from September 2025 — a temporary cut matching what federal and Flemish MPs already accepted.
BXL-2425-00031-v13.proposed_by: Bertin Mampaka Mankamba (president of the Parliament, on behalf of the Bureau — broad cross-party consensus: MR, Groen, Les Engagés, Open Vld, N-VA and others)
BXL-2425-00031-v13.source_brief:
The Brussels Parliament's Bureau — after weeks of negotiations — agreed to introduce a 5% retention on every MP's base parliamentary indemnity from September 2025, matching the temporary reduction already applied by the federal Chamber and the Flemish Parliament. It is part of a wider package cutting the Parliament's own budget by 10%.

- **What it does:** removes 5% from the base indemnity from the first payment of the 2025-2026 session; the savings go to the Parliament's general running costs; this follows an already-applied series of Bureau measures (no chauffeured car for the president, no phone reimbursement for Bureau members, no benefits for honorary MPs).
- **The institutional backdrop:** Brussels MPs are cited as the best-paid regional legislators in Belgium at over 7,000 euros net per month; the regional budget runs a deficit of 1.6–1.9 billion euros; the Parliament's own 2025 budget reached 14 provisional twelfths (approx. 69 million euros), up from 57 million in 2024.
- **The political story:** an opposition group had been demanding a 5% cut for seven months; the Bureau brought its own version on the same day; the rival text (A-103) was put to the vote first, then this Bureau text — two near-identical cuts, two separate roll-calls.
- **The rub:** whether a 5% temporary reduction on base pay — excluding special-function indemnities — is a meaningful gesture of solidarity or a carefully scoped minimum that leaves the best-paid chamber in Belgium largely untouched.
deep_facts: The text is proposition de decision A-150/1 – 2024/2025, tabled by the president on behalf of the Bureau after a Bureau agreement reached on 9 July 2025, the day before the plenary (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The 5% retention applies to the parliamentary indemnity as defined in the 1989 Council of Brussels-Capital Region decision and its subsequent amendments; the product of the retention is allocated to the Parliament's general expenditure (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The Bureau's framing aligns Brussels on the federal Chamber and Flemish Parliament, both of which temporarily reduced their members' indemnity to 95% of the base salary of a 'conseiller d'Etat sans anciennete'; Brussels MPs' base indemnity had been set at 100% of that reference salary (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Brussels MPs' net monthly indemnity is cited as 'plus de 7.000 euros', described by several speakers as the highest parliamentary pay in Belgium; the Parliament's 2025 budget on provisional twelfths reached approximately 69 million euros, compared to 57–59 million in 2024 (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The wider Bureau savings package — supported by a majority of MR, Groen, Les Engages, Open Vld and N-VA — targets a 10% reduction in Parliament spending, bringing the budget toward 62 million euros; it includes measures already applied: no chauffeured presidential car, no honorary-MP benefits, no phone reimbursements for Bureau members and group chairs, no support for the outgoing president (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

PTB's two amendments to A-150 were voted separately: Amendment 1 (removing the 'temporary' qualifier from the text) was voted and rejected (vote 10); Amendment 2 (applying the 5% cut also to special-function indemnities) was voted and rejected (vote 12); both were defeated before the Bureau text itself came to its final vote (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The competing PTB/PVDA text A-103 — which would have made the cut permanent (definitive) and extended it to special-function indemnities — was put to the vote in the same sitting, before the Bureau text A-150 (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The regional deficit is cited at 1.6 to 1.9 billion euros for 2025, with a consolidated regional debt described as 'avoisinant les 16,5 milliards d'euros'; cited parallel austerity measures include a 15% cut in association budgets and removal of a 10-euro supplement in family allowances for children born before 1 December 2019 (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Ecolo and Team Fouad Ahidar stated they considered the PTB text more coherent and linear but indicated they would support the Bureau text; Groen said it was not opposed to A-103 but chose to respect the broader cross-party Bureau accord; cd&v, not represented on the Bureau, also backed the 5% cut while regretting it did not extend to supplementary indemnities (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

DeFI noted it is not represented on the Bureau, raised the question of the 2014 rule change allowing a single member to constitute a group and draw group-chair special-function pay, and called for a wider debate on the financing of parliamentary activity (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
BXL-2425-00031-v13.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The sequence — the opposition text put to the vote first, the Bureau text right after — is the cleanest illustration of consensus politics: the majority uses the opposition's own language (5% cut) while stripping out the elements it finds inconvenient (permanence, special functions), then claims the moral credit for chamber-wide agreement.
- 'Temporary' is doing significant political work here: it leaves the door open for the cut to quietly expire, or for a later interparlementary negotiation to reset the baseline — a flexibility the Bureau majority clearly values more than the PTB's structural permanence.
- The exclusion of special-function indemnities is a material choice: it protects the pay of Bureau members and group chairs — precisely the people who negotiated the deal — while presenting the cut as universal.
- A broad final endorsement after a heated debate would not be consensus on substance; it is consensus on the symbol — every party can tell voters it supported a parliamentary pay cut, while the disagreement about its scope disappears from the record.
BXL-2425-00031-v13.raw_fr: La proposition de decision A-150/1 – 2024/2025, soumise par le Bureau au nom d'un large consensus entre groupes, introduit une retenue temporaire de 5 % sur l'indemnite parlementaire de base des membres du Parlement bruxellois a partir du premier paiement de la session 2025-2026. Elle s'inscrit dans un effort plus large de reduction du budget du Parlement de 10 % et aligne Bruxelles sur la Chambre des representants et le Parlement flamand, qui avaient deja reduit temporairement leurs indemnites a 95 % du traitement de reference.
